body_markdown:
In most hotels, ordering food to your room still runs on a phone call and a printed menu. Someone writes the order down, the kitchen gets a ticket, and the charge is posted to the room to be settled at checkout.


That process works, which is probably why few operators look closely at what it costs them. This article looks at where the cost sits, what changes when the menu becomes a QR code the guest scans and pays through, and what to decide before switching.


## **In-room dining or room service?**


In practice the two terms mean the same operation. Over the last decade or so, many hotels renamed room service to in-room dining, partly to position it as a restaurant-quality meal rather than a late-night convenience, and partly because "service" had come to be read as "surcharge" by guests. Whatever a property calls it, the mechanics are identical: a guest orders food to the room, the kitchen prepares it, someone carries it up, and the hotel has to get paid for it.


The name matters less than the economics, so that is where the rest of this piece spends its time.


## **What room service costs a hotel**


Start with the visible costs. Someone has to answer the phone, a runner has to be available, and the kitchen stays staffed for a small number of late orders because the menu promises 24-hour availability.


Hotel appraiser David Sangree,[writing for Hospitality Net](https://www.hospitalitynet.org/opinion/4061974/room-service-more-than-a-revenue-generator?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) , described that around-the-clock promise as the source of "particularly inefficient labor management" and found that about one in five of the hotels his firm appraised ran room service at a loss, with urban properties the most likely to lose money on it because of labor costs. Room service was also a small line in his data, at around 1.2% of total hotel revenue.


The folio is the larger cost. Charging food to the room means the hotel extends credit on every order and collects at checkout, and any charge the guest later disputes becomes a chargeback.


[Elavon puts the average chargeback ratio](https://www.elavon.com/resources/insights/mastering-chargeback-management-in-hospitality.html?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) for travel and hospitality at 0.89% to 2.0% of transactions, with each case costing the merchant around $25 to $30 on top of the refunded amount, and it identifies first-party fraud, where the cardholder disputes a legitimate charge, as the largest fraud threat merchants now face.


Small F&B charges are the hardest to defend because the records behind them are often incomplete; dispute specialists list[unclear incidental receipts](https://www.chargeflow.io/blog/hotel-chargebacks?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) among the most common gaps in a hotel's evidence.


None of these problems is dramatic on its own. Together they explain why room service tends to be the first thing an operator cuts when margins tighten.


## **What changes when the menu is a QR code**


The alternative that hotels are moving to is simple enough to describe in a sentence. A QR code on the desk or the TV opens the menu in the guest's phone browser, the guest orders and pays there, and the order appears in the kitchen with the room number attached.


A few things change as a result, and most of them are operational rather than technical.


### **The menu becomes live**


Mark a dish unavailable and it disappears from every room at once. Show a smaller late-night menu after 10pm. Raise prices for the holiday weekend without reprinting anything. Add a photo to the dish you want to sell more of.


### **Errors fall because the guest typed the order**


No handoff from phone to notepad to kitchen. Modifiers, allergies, and "no ice" survive the trip. The guest sees exactly what they ordered and what it cost before they confirm.


### **The phone stops being a bottleneck**


The front desk at 11pm is no longer an order line, and a kitchen can take ten orders in the same minute without anyone being on hold.


### **The order is paid before it is cooked**


This is the change that affects the finance side. The guest pays by card, GCash, Maya, or QR Ph at the moment they order. The charge never touches the folio, so checkout is quicker, there is nothing to dispute at the desk, and the chargeback exposure on a tray of club sandwiches goes away. A guest who is not staying at the hotel, such as a day-pass visitor, can order the same way because there is no folio to depend on.


### **Foreign guests pay with their own cards**


A visitor from Seoul or Sydney does not need to install a local e-wallet to order breakfast. They tap their Visa or Mastercard and are charged in pesos. For properties in Boracay, Cebu, or Palawan, where a large share of guests are international, this alone removes a recurring friction point.


Operators who run QR ordering often report that average order sizes go up once guests can browse photos and add items without feeling rushed by someone waiting on the line. Results vary by property and by menu, so treat that as something to measure rather than assume.


What QR ordering does not change is also worth saying plainly. Someone still has to carry the food upstairs. The kitchen still has to be good. A guest who prefers to pick up the phone should still be able to, and the hotels that do this well keep the phone line open and let the QR code become the default rather than the only path.

## **QR code ordering for the hotel restaurants and amenities**


Once the menu lives on a QR code, the same setup works in every food and drink outlet on the property, from the restaurant to the sunbeds.


Poolside and beachfront service is the obvious next one. A sunbed has no table number and the guest usually has no wallet with them, so a code on the umbrella or the cabana card lets them order a drink and pay from the lounger. The order carries the location, so the runner knows where to go.


The resort restaurant benefits for a different reason. Large tables want to split the bill, and a QR at the table lets each guest pay for their own share without a server running three cards. The spa, the kids' club snack bar, and the conference coffee station all work the same way: a code, a menu, a payment, and no folio reconciliation afterwards.

## **Booking tours and activities through the same QR code**


Food is the obvious use, but the same code can sell anything the property schedules. A tour desk menu can list island-hopping trips, spa treatments, kayak rentals, or a sunset cruise, with the date and time slot chosen as part of the order. The guest books and pays from the lounger or the room instead of queueing at the concierge desk, and the operator gets a confirmed, paid booking with the guest's details attached.


Paying at the time of booking changes the economics of activities in the same way it changes in-room dining. A no-show on a prepaid slot no longer costs the operator the seat, and there is no deposit to chase or refund to argue about at checkout. For properties that work with outside tour operators, the booking record also gives both sides the same list of who paid for what.


For the hotel, the result is that food and beverage revenue from every corner of the property shows up in one place, paid and settled, instead of being scattered across room charges, cash drawers, and a card terminal at the pool bar.

## **Before you switch: the questions worth asking**


Rolling this out is less a technology project than an operations one. These are the decisions that tend to matter.


### **Does it need to integrate with our property management system?**


For food and drink that is paid at the time of order, no, and that is the point. The folio keeps doing what it is good at (the room, incidentals, deposits) and F&B settles on its own. Some properties want certain outlets to keep posting to the room, which is fine; decide outlet by outlet rather than all at once.


### **Who receives the order, and how fast?**


A tablet in the kitchen, a printer, or a notification on a manager's phone. Decide who accepts an order, what the guest sees while they wait, and what the promised delivery time is. The guest's experience of "fast" starts the moment they tap pay.


### **What goes on the card in the room?**


The QR code needs a sentence of explanation and a reason to use it. "Scan to see tonight's menu and order in two minutes" works better than a bare code with a logo. Many properties put the same code on the TV welcome screen and in the pre-arrival email.


### **How do you design the menu for a phone?**


Fewer items at night, photos on the dishes that carry margin, dietary tags, and a clear line for any tray charge or service charge. Under Philippine law, service charges collected from guests must be distributed in full to employees, so if you add one, show it upfront rather than at the end.


### **Which payment methods do your guests actually use?**


Domestic travelers lean on GCash, Maya, and QR Ph. International guests want to tap a card. Make sure both groups can pay without a workaround. If QR Ph is new to your team,[this explainer on how QR Ph works](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/what-is-qrph?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) covers the basics.


### **Do you keep the phone?**


Yes. Keep it for guests who prefer it, for accessibility, and for special requests that do not fit a menu. The goal is to move most orders off the phone, not to remove the option.

## **Frequently asked questions**


#### ****What is the difference between in-room dining and room service?****


There is no operational difference. In-room dining is the name many hotels adopted for room service to signal a restaurant-quality meal delivered to the room. The process, the staffing, and the billing are the same unless the hotel changes how orders are placed and paid.


#### ****Do guests need to download an app to order through a QR code?****


No. With PayMongo Order & Pay, the QR code opens the menu in the phone's web browser. The guest orders and pays there, with no app, account, or sign-up required.


#### ****Can orders still be charged to the room?****


Orders placed through Order & Pay are paid at the time of ordering, so they do not post to the folio. Hotels that want certain outlets to keep charging to the room can continue to do so through their property management system and use QR ordering for the outlets where paid-at-order makes more sense, such as the pool, the beach, or late-night in-room dining.


#### ****What payment methods can guests use?****


Visa and Mastercard, including international cards charged in pesos, plus GCash, Maya, QR Ph, and online banking. Guests choose their method at the end of the order.


#### ****Does QR ordering work with our hotel's property management system?****


It works alongside it. Order & Pay handles food and beverage orders that are paid on the spot, and your PMS continues to manage rooms, deposits, and incidentals. There is no integration required to get started.
